clinical_knowledge.topic: Left Atrial Myxoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Left Atrial Myxoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt surgical resection via median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass, excising the tumor with a margin of the atrial septum at its attachment site to prevent recurrence, without delaying for the risk of embolization or sudden mitral inflow obstruction, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic syncope and severe shortness of breath when sitting up, with tumor plop on heart exam

Key HPI features: 49F presenting with posture-dependent syncope and low-grade fever where 2D echocardiogram reveals a large, pedunculated gelatinous mass attached to the fossa ovalis in left atrium prolapsing across mitral valve.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.8C, HR 92, BP 118/74, symptoms and murmur intensity vary with position. Auscultation reveals a low-pitched early diastolic sound ('tumor plop') following S2, with a variable diastolic murmur that changes with posture. Labs show mild anemia and elevated ESR/CRP. 2D and transesophageal echocardiogram confirm a large, pedunculated gelatinous mass attached to the fossa ovalis in the left atrium, prolapsing across the mitral valve during diastole and intermittently obstructing left ventricular inflow.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Left Atrial Myxoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mitral stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope that changes with position — a classic clue to a mobile obstructing mass.
management_principles: Arrange prompt cardiothoracic surgical resection via median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass, excising the tumor with a margin of the atrial septum at its attachment site to prevent recurrence
Avoid delaying surgery given the risk of systemic embolization or sudden fatal mitral inflow obstruction
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 49F presenting with posture-dependent syncope, severe shortness of breath when sitting up, and low-grade fever, found on echocardiogram to have a large pedunculated left atrial mass prolapsing across the mitral valve.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.8C, HR 92, BP 118/74, symptoms and murmur intensity vary with position. Auscultation reveals a low-pitched early diastolic sound ('tumor plop') following S2, with a variable diastolic murmur that changes with posture. Labs show mild anemia and elevated ESR/CRP. 2D and transesophageal echocardiogram confirm a large, pedunculated gelatinous mass attached to the fossa ovalis in the left atrium, prolapsing across the mitral valve during diastole and intermittently obstructing left ventricular inflow.
reference_soap.assessment: Left atrial myxoma causing intermittent, posture-dependent mitral inflow ("ball-valve") obstruction, with associated constitutional symptoms.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange prompt cardiothoracic surgical resection via median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass, excising the tumor with a margin of the atrial septum at its attachment site to prevent recurrence. Avoid delaying surgery given the risk of systemic embolization or sudden fatal mitral inflow obstruction.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic triad of left atrial myxoma: positional obstructive symptoms (syncope/dyspnea), constitutional symptoms mimicking infection, and embolic phenomena
Formulate a prioritized differential diagnosis for a left atrial mass, including mitral stenosis, left atrial thrombus, and other cardiac tumors
Select and interpret echocardiography (2D and transesophageal) to characterize the mass, its attachment site, and its effect on mitral inflow
Explain why prompt surgical excision, including a margin of the atrial septum at the attachment site, is required regardless of symptom severity

teaching.one_liner: A benign but dangerous gelatinous tumor attached to the atrial septum can prolapse across the mitral valve, causing posture-dependent obstruction to blood flow with syncope and breathlessness worse when sitting up.
red_flags: Syncope that changes with position — a classic clue to a mobile obstructing mass

must_ask.say: Does your breathlessness or fainting change depending on your position — like sitting up versus lying down?
Can you describe what happens during the fainting spells?
Have you had any low-grade fevers or fatigue?
How long has this been going on?
Any sudden weakness, vision changes, or limb pain that could suggest a piece broke off?

history.answer: I keep passing out and losing consciousness, especially when I sit up in bed, and it feels like I suddenly cannot catch my breath.
It almost always happens right as I sit upright from lying down in bed or getting off the couch.
It has never happened while exercising, and if I stay completely flat on my back, I feel much better and do not pass out.
Right before I go out, I feel intensely lightheaded and my vision darkens, but I do not get cold sweats or nausea.
I develop sudden, suffocating shortness of breath right when I sit up, but there is no heavy or crushing chest pain.
It happens strictly when I move into an upright position; it has never happened from coughing, straining on the toilet, or standing in warm crowds.
My husband says I was out cold for less than a minute, probably around thirty or forty seconds.
He told me my whole body went limp, with no stiffening, jerking of my limbs, or rolling back of my eyes.
No, I did not bite my tongue or the inside of my cheeks, and I have not lost control of my bladder.
The moment I came to on the floor, I was completely alert and clear-headed right away without any confusion.
I scraped my left elbow on the nightstand during the last fall, but thankfully I did not hit my head.
No, I have not had any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, slurred speech, or vision loss.
This started about a month ago and has happened three times, but the severe dizziness when sitting up happens almost every day.
I have had a mild, low-grade fever on and off for the past few weeks, along with feeling unusually tired and drained.
I have not had any nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dark black stools, and I have been drinking fluids regularly.
I eat three balanced meals every day and do not have diabetes or low blood sugar issues.
I have never had any heart murmurs, valve problems, or cardiac conditions diagnosed before.
I honestly feel like something inside my heart is physically blocking the blood flow when I sit up, and I am terrified of fainting again without warning.
I'm terrified I'm going to faint while driving my car or when I'm alone in the house and crack my head open.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, or any other long-term medical conditions.
I have never had any surgery or been admitted to a hospital before.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of red wine with dinner once or twice a month.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my husband.
My menstrual cycles are regular every 28 days, my last period was two weeks ago, and there is no chance I am pregnant.
Both of my parents are healthy in their seventies, and no one in my family has had sudden cardiac death or unexplained fainting.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and body temperature 37.8°C.
Supine blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg with heart rate 92 bpm; upon standing, blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg with heart rate 96 bpm, showing no orthostatic hypotension.
Alert woman resting comfortably while supine, but becomes visibly short of breath and distressed upon sitting upright.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted bilaterally without scleral icterus.
Oral cavity is clear with moist pink mucosa and no lateral tongue biting marks or pharyngeal injection.
Auscultation reveals a prominent low-pitched early diastolic sound following S2 and a variable diastolic murmur that becomes significantly louder when sitting upright.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal breath sounds and no crackles or wheezes.
Radial and pedal pulses are regular, symmetric, and full bilaterally with no blood pressure disparity between arms.
Skin is warm and intact with no peripheral emboli, petechiae, or splinter hemorrhages, and only a minor faint scrape on the left elbow.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial expression and normal eye movements.
Muscle strength is 5/5 throughout all four extremities with normal tone and no focal neurological deficit.
